gameVerifiedNote: Interop metadata and the same build's dump.cs only. No method was invoked, no hook was installed, no game was started and no method body was decoded for this document, so every entry below is a signature, a field offset or a namespace fact. The three questions that need a method body are in `unverified` and are the game-internal confirmation list for this slice.

dump.note: Signatures, field offsets and RVAs of build 20403457; the local copy was read from the repository's own frozen artifact, not re-dumped.

scope: The one native modification entry ForgeMap's `forge.action.combat.attribute_apply` writes through, the clear entry `attribute_remove` and the cleanup paths use, the tables both are keyed by, and the enum the `attribute` port resolves against. This provider is the `gtfo.player` owner, so the evidence is about the `Agent`-keyed modification table and not about any enemy-only attribute path.

namespaceFacts.claim: `AgentModifier`, `ModifierInstance`, `pModificationInstance` and `AgentModifierManager` are declared in the global namespace of Modules-ASM.dll.
namespaceFacts.basis: ilspycmd -t on the frozen interop emits them with no namespace declaration, while `Agents.Agent` is emitted from `namespace Agents`; the production adapter therefore names them without a using directive.

namespaceFacts.claim: `PlayerAgent` derives from `Agents.Agent`, which is the type every `AgentModifierManager` entry takes.
namespaceFacts.basis: dump.cs 650512 `public class PlayerAgent : Agent, ...`; dump.cs 680534 `public class Agent : MonoBehaviour, ...`

enum.note: Values are not contiguous; nothing may be derived from an index. The catalog's `agent_modifier` set spells each member lower-cased with a case boundary or underscore as a hyphen, and the adapter's table carries this whole enum so a member the shared set drops (`none`) is still recognized and can be refused by name.

types.idTable: `m_modificationIDToAgent` and `m_allModifierInstanceIDs` are the manager's own registration tables; the provider does not read them, because the ledger already holds every id this package handed out and a read of a private table would be a second, weaker record of the same fact.

types.note: The per-agent instance the manager keeps: one dictionary of values, one of limits and the modification ids it currently holds.

The synced payload: which agent, which member, the decay rate, the modification id, the original value and the timestamp it was written at. Its shape is evidence that one submission is a sourced contribution with an id, not an absolute assignment.

derivation.claim: `set`, `add` and `subtract` all land as one signed contribution, and `subtract` submits the negated amount.
derivation.basis: the only write entry is `AddSyncedModifierValue(agent, modifier, value, deltaPerSec)`; the row declares no rate port and the entry has no absolute-assignment form, so the three members differ by the sign the modifier table reads as its opposite and by nothing else. A negative value is a real submission in this table: `ModifierInversionSet` and `ModifierHasInvertedMeaning(AgentModifier)` exist because some members (the resistances) mean less of the thing when the value rises.

derivation.claim: A zero return means the entry registered no modification id.
derivation.basis: the return type is the modification id the clear entry takes; a value of 0 is the one value `m_modificationIDToAgent` cannot hold as a real agent index and the one no id-consuming entry could act on. The ruled design lands this as `modifier-id-exhausted` and never invents or retries an id.

derivation.claim: A modification has no native lifetime.
derivation.basis: the payload carries `DeltaPerSec` and `TimeStamp` but no end tick, and no entry takes a duration: the ledger's `ExpiryTick` is Forge's own, cleared through the same native clear an explicit removal uses.

derivation.claim: A request handle is matched to the modification it names through the handle's own identity fields, not through `RuntimeModuleHandle.TryNative`.
derivation.basis: `RuntimeKernel.CleanHandleLifetimes` releases a handle whose registered native object no provider's object resolver recognizes, and this package registers no `PlayerAgent`-recognizing object resolver (`MapObjectModule.Declare` adds entity resolvers and instance resolvers keyed by kind, not object resolvers). Registering the agent would therefore drop a live handle at the next host advance, while the ledger already holds the modification id the handle was minted for.

derivation.claim: `ClearSyncedModifierChange(id)` is the one revoke entry every path uses.
derivation.basis: it is the synced clear the design names for expiry, entity loss and world end, and it is the only clear that reaches the other machines; the unsynced `ClearModifierChange` and the agent-wide `ClearAllModifiersOnAgent` are deliberately unused (see `unusedEntries`).

unusedEntries.why: its bool is the only confirmation the clear family offers, but the ruled design names the synced clear as the revoke entry and forbids a second path; calling both would either double-clear or make the two answers disagree. Recorded here so the omission is a decision, not an oversight.
the unsynced sibling: a write only this machine would see, which is not what a host-owned effect may do.
it clears every modification on an agent, including the booster-implant contributions the game itself wrote; this provider may only release the ids it registered.

it answers the agent's total for one member, which includes every other source's contribution, so it cannot confirm this provider's own write; the result row reports the submitted contribution and the commit state the native return established instead of a total nobody asked about.

hostClientVisibility.write: host-only by construction: the provider's gate is the player identity's own `CanCommit` (registration live, runtime ready, host) and the row is declared `execution: host`, so a client never reaches the native write.
hostClientVisibility.sync: signature-level only: `m_modificationPacket`/`m_modificationClearPacket` and the Send/Receive pairs show the manager has a replication channel for both the modification and its clear, which is why the design chose the synced write and the synced clear. Which end sends has no signature answer.
hostClientVisibility.readback: none on this path: neither `AddSyncedModifierValue` nor `ClearSyncedModifierChange` answers with the state it ended in.

unverified.question: What a zero return from `AddSyncedModifierValue` means besides `no id was registered` (an exhausted counter, a refused modifier, a null agent).
unverified.why: it needs the method body; the local dump carries signatures and RVAs only. The implementation treats zero as a refusal (`modifier-id-exhausted`) and never retries.

unverified.question: Whether `AddSyncedModifierValue` sends the packet itself and whether the host's own client-side application happens on the same call.
unverified.why: needs the bodies of `AddSyncedModifierValue`, `SendSyncedModification` and `ReceiveSyncedModification`. The implementation applies on the host and does not attempt a client-side application of its own.

unverified.question: Whether two submissions of the same `(agent, modifier)` pair accumulate, replace or limit each other.
unverified.why: needs `ModifierInstance::AddModifierValue` and `UpdateModifierValues`. The ledger keeps one entry per returned id and never dedupes by `(agent, modifier)`, so whatever the native table does with two ids is what happens.

unverified.question: Whether `ClearSyncedModifierChange` also clears the caller's own copy or only tells the other machines.
unverified.why: needs its body; the remove row's confirmation is the ledger's own (the id was live when the clear was called), which is what the row reports and all it reports.

unverified.question: Whether a modification survives its agent's death, and what a respawned agent's instance holds.
unverified.why: the manager is agent-keyed and no signature says when an entry is dropped. The ledger releases an entity's ids as soon as the player identity stops resolving that life, so no Forge effect outlives the life it was written on regardless of what the native table does.

gameVerificationPlan: Apply one modifier to a player and confirm the client sees the attribute change (the sync direction this document cannot answer).
Apply the same modifier twice and read the player's effective value to learn whether two ids accumulate or the last one wins.
Apply with a duration, let it expire, and confirm the value returns to what it was before the first write.
Remove through the handle an apply returned and confirm the value returns to the pre-write reading on every machine.
Apply from a client and confirm the command is rejected with `authority-or-phase` and nothing is written.
